title: Views of self (section 31)
hookLine: views of self and being are not views; so they are called views

cards: Two friends walk out of a movie. One says, that was brilliant. The other says, that was a mess.
By the parking lot, it's no longer about the movie. Each is defending something closer to home: my taste, my judgment, me. A view started as a way of seeing a film and became a wall to stand behind.
Section thirty-one of the Diamond Sutra goes after the view under all the others, the view of a self. And it doesn't swap it for a better view. It does something quieter.

teach.h: DID HE TEACH A VIEW OF SELF?
teach.b: The Buddha asks Subhuti, in paraphrase: if someone said the Tathagata taught a view of a self, a being, a living soul, a person, would they be speaking rightly? No, says Subhuti.

teach.h: NO VIEW, SO CALLED A VIEW.
teach.b: What the Tathagata taught as a view of self is taught as no view, and that is why it's called a view of self.
The same four ideas the sutra has cut since its opening sections come back one last time, and this time it isn't the self being cut. It's the view of it.
Then the Buddha says that one who sets out on this path should know all things, see all things, and trust all things in such a way that they don't hold on to even an idea of a thing.

teach.h: NOT EVEN AN IDEA OF A THING.
teach.b: And of course: an idea of a thing is no idea; that's why it's called an idea. Even the sutra's own teaching about no self is not a new belief to clutch.

teach.h: THE WEEK: THE GRIP, NOT THE THING.
teach.b: Look back at the week. No beings freed: help without the ledger. Form and sound: not the face or the voice.
Not annihilation, and still not nothing. Merit not held. Neither coming nor going.
Now views of self. Every day the blade had the same edge. It doesn't throw away beings, bodies, merit or worlds.
It takes away the grip. Today it reaches a deeper one: the grip on being right about who we are.

how: Mahayana teachers read section 31 of the Diamond Sutra as a warning not to turn the teaching of no self into one more view to defend; students meet it in chanting, study and meditation on how views are held.

o: how other people see you and judge your character
a rule that you must never share your opinions
a view of self, taught as no view, so only called one

p: no idea, so called an idea
without holding an idea of a thing
takes the grip, not the thing

s: the sutra swaps the view of self for a better view
it calls the view of self no view, and won't let even an idea of a thing be clutched.
Subhuti says the Tathagata didn't teach a view of self
what he taught as a view of self is taught as no view, so it's called one.
the bodhisattva is told to stop knowing things
they know, see and trust all things, without holding an idea of a thing.

games.q: you're Subhuti. someone says the Tathagata taught a view of self, of a being, of a soul, of a person. are they right?
o: no: a view of self is taught as no view
partly: he taught only the view of a person
games.why: Subhuti says no: what was taught as a view of self is taught as no view, and that's why it's called a view of self.

practice: Pick up one opinion you hold firmly, about a person, a habit, a team, or yourself, and let it sit in your mind like a stone in an open palm. Notice where it presses: the jaw, the chest, the hands.
Don't drop it and don't argue with it; just loosen the fingers, and let the breath move around it.

wordCard.voice: Views of self. Section thirty-one: what the Tathagata taught as a view of self is taught as no view, and so it's called a view. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit (Pali ditthi): a view, a way of seeing; in section 31, the 'view of self' that is no view.

carryVoice: Your line: so-called views. A view held in an open palm, not a fist. That's day one thousand one hundred forty-eight, and that's the week.
